Here is a careful English translation, line by line. Some passages are damaged or uncertain, so I mark those as such.

1. **When day had gone forth, when day had been fashioned from the horizon of heaven and earth,**  
2. **when night had gone forth, when night had been fashioned from the horizon of heaven and earth,**  
3. **when the year had gone forth, when fate had been determined for the year,**  
4. **when the Anunna gods had been brought into being,**  
5. **when for Inana the divine offices were assigned,**  
6. **when Inana kept moving about in heaven and on earth,**  
7. **when Inana […] had made ready and given birth,**  
8. **when the gods of the sheepfold/settlement were bound fast to their city(?) — uncertain,**  
9. **when the great gods all sat in their places, and the lesser gods were carrying the toil-baskets,**  
10. **when the gods were digging out the rivers, heaping up their earth into embankments,**  
11. **when the gods were scattering the clay, and were setting living beings in place by command,**  
12. **at that time there were broad understanding and wise counsel among all the great gods.**  
13. **Enki, in the depths of the Apsu, in that place among the gods, in its very heart, brought forth wondrous things.**  
14. **He lay down in his bedchamber and did not rise from sleep.**  
15. **The gods were weeping before him, making supplication with tears.**  
16. **Because he lay asleep in the holy place, he did not rise from his bed.**  
17. **Namma, the mother who gave birth to the princely Anunna gods,**  
18. **brought the tears of the gods before her son.**  
19. **[…] caused him to lie there indeed, and indeed caused him to keep sleeping,**  
20. **[…] he did not rise,**  
21. **“O my creator, whose hands fashioned all the divine powers, […] they have pressed upon your neck(?)” — very uncertain.**

A few notes:
- This is from the **Sumerian creation context associated with Enki and Namma**, likely from the opening of **“Enki and Ninmah”** or a closely related composition.
- Lines **7, 8, 19, 20, and 21** are fragmentary and cannot be translated with confidence.
- Terms like **Anunna**, **Apsu/Engur**, and **divine offices/me** are culturally specific and sometimes have no exact one-word English equivalent.
